deep.reconstruction:
PART A (end of an argument begun on the previous page). The previous page sketches a direct proof of Picard's little theorem 'without the help of modular functions'. Let f be entire with infinitely many simple zeros. Consider the level curves |f(z)| = m as m increases from 0. For small m they are disjoint small analytic ovals around the zeros. When two ovals meet, the meeting point is a zero of f', and it moves analytically as m grows. The resulting cells, with the critical points of f as corners, are supposed to tile the plane. In each cell f should be univalent, apart from at most two omitted values, as in the model f = e^z - 1, for which |f|^2 = e^{2x} - 2 e^x cos y + 1 = m. This page continues: 'The region can reach to infinity only with 2 ends. If every region with 2 ends is to reach only to infinity, then it cannot happen that 3 regions meet at one point A, as in the figure. The figure shows a horizontal level line, region 1 above, regions 2 and 3 separated by a vertical segment ending at A, and regions 4 and 5 beside them. Otherwise the function would have to have a branch point at A, which is excluded.' In modern terms: a point where three cells of the level-set decomposition meet would force the local inverse of f to be branched at A in a way not allowed for a single-valued f. The argument is heuristic. It does not show that the cells exhaust the plane, that f is univalent on each cell, or why each cell has at most 2 ends. These are exactly the hard parts of Picard's theorem.

PART B (new theorem). Claim: let a countable set {x_1, x_2, ...} of reals (implicitly in [0,1], since 0 and 1 serve as endpoints) be given, with prescribed values f(x_k). Then there is a series of polynomials, sum_n (G_n - G_{n-1}) with G_0 = 0, that converges at each x_k to f(x_k). Construction (finished on the next page):
(1) Let L_1 be the polygon 0 - x_1 - 1.
(2) Insert x_2. If x_1 < x_2 < 1, L_2 is the zigzag 0 - x_1 - x_2 - 1.
(3) If 0 < x_3 < x_1, L_3 is 0 - x_3 - x_1 - x_2 - 1, and so on.
Thus L_n is the piecewise-linear interpolant of the data at x_1..x_n. The values at 0 and 1 must be fixed somehow, e.g. 0 (my assumption). Next, choose polynomials G_n with sup_[0,1] |G_n - L_n| < eps_n and eps_n -> 0. This uses Runge/Weierstrass polygon approximation (Runge, Acta Math. 7, p. 387). Then f(x) = G_1 + (G_2 - G_1) + (G_3 - G_2) + ... has n-th partial sum G_n. For n >= k we have L_n(x_k) = f(x_k), hence |G_n(x_k) - f(x_k)| < eps_n -> 0. So the series converges at every x_k to the prescribed value [convergence step mine, implicit in the text].

Next-page consequences:
(a) If {x_k} is dense and f is continuous, L_n -> f uniformly, which yields Weierstrass's theorem.
(b) For Thomae's function f(p/q) = 1/q, f(irrational) = 0, with {x_k} the rationals, L_n(x) -> 0 at irrational x. The neighbours of x eventually have large denominators. So the series converges on all of [0,1] to a function with a dense set of discontinuities. [Justification of (b) mine.]
errors: Part A is only a heuristic sketch. Three steps are asserted without proof: that the cells cover the plane, that f is univalent on each cell, and that each cell reaches infinity with at most 2 ends. These carry the whole content of Picard's theorem.

The 'branch point' argument at A is unclear as stated. At a simple critical point of f, level curves of |f| do cross and cells do meet. The exclusion must rest on the extra hypothesis about 2-ended cells, which is not justified.
Part B: the values at the endpoints 0 and 1 are not specified unless 0 and 1 are among the given points. The restriction to [0,1], or to a bounded interval, is implicit.

Part B is correct, but if only convergence at the countably many points is wanted, the detour is unnecessary. The Lagrange interpolation polynomials P_n through (x_1, f(x_1)), ..., (x_n, f(x_n)) already satisfy P_n(x_k) = f(x_k) exactly for n >= k. The zigzag construction pays off only for the extra claims of convergence on the whole interval (the Weierstrass and Thomae applications).
In Part B, convergence off the given points is not claimed on this page. In general it fails without extra hypotheses.

results.what: Heuristic level-curve (|f| = m) decomposition approach to Picard's little theorem: cells are fundamental regions of univalence, no triple junctions because there are no branch points
results.modern_name: Picard's little theorem (attempted elementary/topological proof via level sets; related to the line-complex/Speiser-graph picture of Riemann surfaces)
results.usually_credited_to: Picard 1879 (modular function proof); elementary proofs by Borel 1896; level-set/line-complex ideas by Speiser and Nevanlinna, 1920s-30s

results.what: Any function on a countable subset of [0,1] is the pointwise limit on that set of a series of polynomials, built by approximating successive piecewise-linear interpolants
results.modern_name: Pointwise polynomial interpolation/approximation on countable sets; polygon approximation in the style of Runge's proof of the Weierstrass approximation theorem
results.usually_credited_to: Weierstrass 1885, Runge 1885 (Acta Math. 7); the countable-set statement is folklore

results.what: Application: Thomae's function is the everywhere-pointwise limit of a polynomial series on [0,1] (next page)
results.modern_name: Thomae's function is of Baire class 1

deep.surprise_reason: The Picard sketch is heuristic and incomplete. The interpolation theorem is close to Runge's 1885 polygon method, whose paper Hilbert cites. The mildly notable point is Hilbert's (pre-Baire) observation that a function with a dense set of discontinuities, such as Thomae's, is the pointwise limit of polynomials. That is a minor unpublished remark, not a major result.
